title: Diabetes Mellitus: Glucose Monitoring, Hypoglycemia, Sick-Day Care and Complication Prevention
html:
Diabetes care is more than lowering one glucose number. The RN coordinates safe monitoring, nutrition and medication timing, prevents hypoglycemia, recognizes illness-related deterioration, and supports protection of the heart, kidneys, eyes, nerves, and feet. Goals must fit the person's diabetes type, age, functional status, comorbidities, hypoglycemia risk, and own priorities.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish the major care implications of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
  • Interpret blood glucose, A1C, and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in context.
  • Respond safely to mild and severe hypoglycemia and prevent recurrence.
  • Coordinate inpatient insulin with meals, procedures, and changing intake.
  • Teach individualized sick-day actions and red flags for hyperglycemic crisis.
  • Assess and support cardiovascular, kidney, retinal, neuropathy, and foot-risk prevention.

Understand the type, treatment, and context

Type 1 diabetes involves profound insulin deficiency and requires ongoing insulin replacement. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance and progressive insulin-secretory dysfunction; treatment may include nutrition and activity changes, noninsulin medicines, insulin, and therapies selected for cardiovascular or kidney benefit. Other forms and pregnancy-related diabetes require distinct plans. Never assume that a person using insulin has type 1 diabetes, or that a person with type 2 diabetes cannot develop a severe insulin-deficiency crisis.

At every encounter, identify the usual regimen, insulin delivery device, last doses, meals, activity, recent glucose pattern, episodes of low blood glucose, awareness of symptoms, kidney function, steroid or infection exposure, ability to obtain supplies, and ability to perform the plan. Ask what the person does when sick and whether they have access to a glucose meter, CGM supplies, rapid carbohydrate, and prescribed glucagon.

Read glucose data as a pattern

A1C estimates average glycemia over roughly two to three months but does not show daily lows and may be misleading when red-cell turnover is altered, including some anemias, transfusion, advanced kidney disease, or pregnancy. For many nonpregnant adults, an A1C goal below 7% is appropriate, but a safer or different goal may be needed when hypoglycemia, frailty, comorbidity, or treatment burden outweighs benefit. CGM adds time-in-range and low-glucose information; review trends and symptoms rather than a single point.

CGM measures interstitial glucose and can lag behind blood glucose when values change rapidly. If symptoms do not match a sensor reading, the device is warming up, transmission fails, or accuracy is in doubt, use an available blood glucose meter according to the person's plan. In the hospital, follow facility-approved point-of-care confirmation and treatment protocols. Document the value with timing relative to food, insulin, steroids, exercise, and symptoms.

Safety before a target
A seemingly excellent A1C can hide repeated hypoglycemia. Ask about lows and review CGM or meter data, function, and the client's ability to carry out the plan.

Hypoglycemia requires immediate action

A blood glucose below 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia. Early signs can include sweating, shakiness, hunger, palpitations, anxiety, and headache; neuroglycopenia may cause confusion, behavior change, seizure, or unconsciousness. Some people have few warning symptoms. Confirm a value when feasible without delaying treatment of a symptomatic person and look for common causes: too much insulin or secretagogue, missed or delayed food, increased activity, alcohol, kidney dysfunction, or a change in nutrition or steroid therapy.

For an alert adult who can swallow safely, use the individual's plan or approved protocol; a common approach is 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if still below 70 mg/dL. Once corrected, provide a meal or snack if needed to prevent recurrence and identify the cause. Never give food or drink to a person unable to swallow safely. Severe hypoglycemia with seizure, unconsciousness, or inability to self-treat requires emergency help and prescribed glucagon or IV glucose under protocol, airway protection, repeated checks, and evaluation of recurrent risk.

Coordinate inpatient care with nutrition

Hospital glucose goals differ from outpatient A1C goals. Current ADA guidance recommends approximately 100–180 mg/dL for many noncritically ill adults when achievable without significant hypoglycemia and 140–180 mg/dL for most critically ill adults receiving treatment. The actual order and target should be individualized. Persistent hyperglycemia needs treatment and cause assessment; overly tight control can cause harm.

For clients eating reliably, coordinated basal, prandial, and correction insulin is commonly used. When intake is poor or absent, basal plus correction may be used as ordered. Check whether meal trays arrived, food was eaten, tube feeds or IV nutrition were interrupted, or a procedure changed timing before giving prandial insulin. Do not independently omit all basal insulin in a person with type 1 diabetes who is not eating; communicate and follow a safe, adjusted plan because insulin deficiency can lead to ketoacidosis. Review steroids, infection, dialysis, kidney injury, and discharge changes with the prescribing team.

Sick days need a written plan

Illness can raise glucose even when appetite falls. Teach the person to follow their individualized sick-day plan for checking glucose more often, maintaining appropriate fluids and carbohydrates, using medicines safely, and checking ketones when advised. People with type 1 diabetes generally need continued basal insulin during illness, though doses may require clinician-guided adjustment. A person taking an SGLT2 inhibitor may develop ketoacidosis with less marked hyperglycemia; new nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or deep breathing warrants urgent evaluation regardless of a seemingly modest glucose reading.

Escalate for persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, positive or rising ketones per the plan, labored breathing, confusion, severe weakness, or persistent high glucose despite prescribed corrective actions. A forthcoming lesson covers DKA and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state in detail. The RN does not improvise insulin doses or advise the client to stop all medicine without a prescribed plan.

Prevent complications across organ systems

Glycemia, blood pressure, lipids, smoking cessation, movement, nutrition, and appropriate medications all contribute to cardiovascular and kidney risk reduction. Arrange periodic estimated GFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio according to the individualized plan; kidney injury may be evident through albuminuria before eGFR falls. Review medication dosing and potassium when kidney function changes.

Retinal disease may progress without symptoms, so reinforce scheduled dilated retinal assessment. Screen for neuropathy and inspect feet: skin breaks, calluses, deformity, sensation, pulses, footwear, and healing. A new ulcer, spreading redness, warmth, drainage, discoloration, or a suddenly swollen hot foot needs prompt evaluation. Teach daily self-inspection with help or a mirror when needed, well-fitting footwear, and avoidance of walking barefoot; do not treat a foot wound as routine home care if there are infection or ischemia signs.

Ask about distress, sleep, food security, supplies, cost, vision, dexterity, cognition, language, and support. Diabetes self-management education and support, a dietitian, pharmacy, social work, eye care, podiatry, and kidney or cardiovascular specialists may be appropriate. Make the plan feasible, not merely comprehensive on paper.

Evaluate safety at transitions

Before discharge, reconcile the actual home medicines against inpatient changes, verify that the client can demonstrate glucose checks and medication administration, identify low- and high-glucose actions, has supplies and follow-up, and knows whom to call. If an insulin regimen changes, confirm dose, device, concentration, meal timing, and written instructions. Review the client's understanding with teach-back rather than assuming a prescription is enough.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify diabetes type, regimen, food intake, glucose trend, CGM or meter reliability, symptoms, kidney function, illness, foot findings, and access to supplies.
  2. Analyze cues: Relate glucose changes to insulin, meals, activity, steroids, infection, and kidney function; distinguish sensor mismatch from a true low and identify recurrent risk.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Altered consciousness from hypoglycemia, ketone-associated illness, dehydration, infection, and a limb-threatening foot lesion need urgent attention.
  4. Generate solutions: Treat a low promptly by the safe route, adjust the plan through authorized orders, coordinate meals and medicines, obtain ketone assessment when indicated, and arrange prevention and follow-up.
  5. Take action: Follow glucose and hypoglycemia protocols, never give oral intake to an unsafe swallow, communicate nutrition interruptions and type 1 basal-insulin needs, and teach the written sick-day plan.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Recheck glucose and symptoms, assess recurrence, review time-in-range or A1C in context, confirm foot and kidney follow-up, and use teach-back for the home plan.

Clinical example

A hospitalized client with type 1 diabetes is NPO for a procedure. A meal tray is withheld, but the scheduled prandial insulin remains on the medication list. The RN verifies the current glucose, insulin orders, last basal dose, expected procedure time, and nutrition plan. The RN does not give meal-linked insulin without food or independently stop all basal insulin; the prescriber and diabetes team clarify a safe NPO regimen and monitoring frequency. The RN watches for both hypoglycemia and ketosis as the plan changes.

Original educational synthesis. Individual goals, glucose devices, insulin and other medicine regimens, hypoglycemia treatment, sick-day adjustments, hospital targets, and complication care require current client data, authorized orders, device instructions, local protocols, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official ADA product.
